name: Brindisi
title: Brindisi Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement | Ferries & Tankers
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Brindisi for Greece and Albania ferries, energy-port tankers and bulk carriers: car deck, ramp, tank and deck gauging.
h1: Ship Hull and Deck Gauging in Brindisi, Gateway to Greece
intro: Brindisi is an old Adriatic harbour with a modern working life: ferries to Greece and Albania, tankers serving the industrial and energy zone, and bulk and general cargo ships at the outer quays. Ferry owners want car decks and ramps measured between sailings, and energy-trade ships need deck and tank readings before surveys. Atlantis NDT sends its thickness measurement technicians from India to the ship and plans each job around the sailing timetable and the cargo window.

highlights.p: Ro-pax ships on the Greek and Albanian crossings return on fixed timetables, so car deck, ramp and ballast tank gauging can be divided across several turnarounds without disturbing a single sailing.

Brindisi's petrochemical and energy facilities bring product and chemical tankers and coal and bulk ships, where deck piping, ballast tank and hold readings are tied to survey schedules and charterer checks.

highlights.h: Sheltered harbour with room to work
highlights.p: The outer harbour, protected by breakwaters and an offshore island, gives ships calm berths and anchorage, which makes it easier to plan tanks, decks and piping readings within a fixed working window.

port.h: The port of Brindisi: outer harbour, ferry quays and the industrial zone
p: Brindisi sits on the Adriatic coast of Puglia, near the heel of Italy, and has served the sea route to Greece for more than two thousand years. The modern port is built around a natural harbour with three parts: an outer harbour sheltered by breakwaters and a small island at its mouth, a middle harbour, and an inner basin that reaches towards the old town. Ferry and cruise berths are on the Costa Morena side, while industrial and bulk quays lie along the outer harbour and the eastern shore. Ships approach from open water in the Adriatic through a dredged entrance channel, and the tidal range is small.

The traffic mix splits into passenger shipping and industrial cargo. Ro-pax ferries link Brindisi with Greek ports such as Igoumenitsa and Patras and with Albania, and cruise ships call in season. On the industrial side, the energy and petrochemical zone to the south and east of the city generates tanker calls with refined and chemical products, and coal and other dry bulk have long arrived for the power and industrial users nearby. General cargo and project cargo, including components for energy projects, use the multipurpose quays of the outer harbour.

Gauging demand follows from that split. Ferries accumulate wear on vehicle decks, stern and bow ramps and the ballast tanks below, because trailers, road salt and condensation work on the same steel every day of a season. Tankers and bulk carriers behave as they do in any energy port: deck piping, ballast tanks, cofferdams and hold frames drive the survey calendar. Strong northerly winds in winter can delay berthing for a while, and the summer peak on the Greek services leaves ferries with very little spare time alongside, which is why jobs for them are planned in short blocks.

facilities.h: Where gauging happens in Brindisi: ferry berths, tanker jetties and outer quays
p: Ferry gauging takes place at the passenger berths on the Costa Morena side, during turnaround. A ro-pax ship usually has a few hours between disembarkation and the next boarding, and a well-prepared job fits inside that: the vehicle deck is cleared, the ramp is lowered, and readings are taken along marked lines on plating, stiffeners and ramp hinges. Off season, ferries lay by for longer, and the same ship can have its ballast tanks and void spaces measured at leisure. Class surveyors attend when readings are meant for the survey file.

Industrial berths work differently. Tanker jetties in the energy and petrochemical zone apply their own permit rules, so deck and piping gauging goes ahead during cargo operations under the terminal's safety conditions, and entry to cargo tanks is left for a yard. The port has no large commercial drydock of its own, so owners dock ships at yards elsewhere in Italy, Greece, Malta or Croatia, and a measured steel estimate prepared at Brindisi helps the chosen yard to plan renewal. Ships waiting for a berth lie at anchor in the outer roads, where owner's condition checks of accessible spaces are possible in calm weather.
list: Costa Morena ferry berths — vehicle deck plating, stiffeners, ramps and ballast tanks of ro-pax ships gauged during turnaround between sailings
Cruise berths — selected ballast tanks, voids and scrubber lines on cruise ships alongside, between passenger operations
Tanker jetties in the energy and petrochemical zone — deck, deck piping and permitted ballast spaces on product and chemical tankers
Outer harbour bulk and general cargo quays — hold frames, hatch covers and coamings after discharge on coal and dry bulk ships
Outer anchorage — condition checks on ships waiting for a berth or laid up, reached by launch through the ship's agent

context.h: Port state control and regulation for ferry and energy shipping at Brindisi
p: Port state control at Brindisi is carried out by the Italian Coast Guard through the harbour master (Capitaneria di Porto), within the Paris MoU. Ro-pax ferries are additionally subject to the EU's regime of mandatory surveys for regular passenger services, which makes a continuous record of deck and ramp condition useful to owners who must show surveyors that wear is under control. Bulk carriers and tankers face ESP requirements, and the ship risk profile decides how often an older vessel is boarded. Structural deficiencies are one of the categories that can lead to detention.

Brindisi's role as a gateway to Greece and Albania has commercial consequences. Ferry operators run old tonnage hard through peak summers, and owners looking at a sale, a charter extension or a refit need credible wall-thickness figures. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation asks ships calling at EU ports to carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime shape the economics of keeping older ships in service. For energy-trade tankers the charterer's vetting inspector also reads the structural record, and a recent set of gauging results saves long discussions.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Brindisi
jobs.p: Brindisi work divides between the ferry timetable and the cargo calendar. Ferry jobs are short, repeatable and planned deck by deck, while tanker and bulk jobs are longer and depend on the terminal's permit conditions. We agree the sequence of spaces, entry permits, surface preparation and report format with the superintendent beforehand, and leave remaining spaces for a later call or a yard stay.

Ballast tank and void space readings on a ferry during winter lay-by, to compile steel estimates before a docking

logistics: Brindisi Airport, Salento, is close to the port, and Bari airport is a longer road alternative with more connections. The ship's agent books ISPS passes and any terminal induction for the tanker jetties and passenger berths. Our technicians are Indian nationals who travel on Schengen visas, so we start the application as the call is confirmed, and fix flights once the ferry's turnaround slot or the tanker's berth time is certain. Because ferries sail on fixed times, a late arrival of the team shortens the work window, which is why we travel a day ahead.
vessels: Ro-pax ferries to Greece and Albania

faqs.q: Can a ferry vehicle deck be gauged between sailings in Brindisi?
faqs.a: Yes, if the job is planned tightly. We fix the zones of the deck in advance, mark lines on the plating, and measure only what the turnaround allows. The next block is picked up on a later call. All readings are combined in a single report, so the surveyor sees a complete record rather than separate partial sets.

faqs.q: Does Brindisi have a drydock for a renewal survey?
faqs.a: Not for large merchant ships. Owners usually book a yard in Italy, Greece, Malta or Croatia. We can gauge the ship at Brindisi beforehand, giving the yard measured steel estimates, then travel to the yard for the full programme so that readings remain comparable from the first estimate to the final report.

faqs.q: Can you measure ramp hinges and ramp plating on a ro-pax ship?
faqs.a: Yes. Ramp plating, stiffeners and the structure around hinges and securing points are measured with the ramp lowered and the area clear of traffic. Surface condition and coating need to be recorded with each reading, and we agree with the ship's crew who prepares the area before the team arrives.

faqs.q: Is gauging possible at the tanker jetties in Brindisi?
faqs.a: For deck, piping and permitted ballast spaces, yes, within the terminal's permit rules. Entry into cargo tanks is not allowed during cargo operations, so cargo tank gauging is planned for a yard stay. The agent arranges terminal access and induction in advance, and we keep the equipment list ready for inspection at the gate.

faqs.q: What happens if winter weather delays a ship at Brindisi?
faqs.a: The job moves with the ship. Strong northerly winds can delay berthing, and we keep the plan flexible, fixing flights only once the berth time is firm. A delayed ferry or tanker often has less time on arrival, so we prioritise the most critical spaces first and leave lower-priority readings for the next call.
